questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go on exchange to an English-speaking city so I could be on the same wavelength as the locals and understand everyone, rather than constantly having to communicate in a language other than my mother tongue. In addition, I wanted to go to a country with great opportunities for running and long coastlines, as well as a culture where I could relatively easily fit in. Sydney turned out to be a perfect match.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Absolutely amazing. It has been the best seven months of my life. Huge recommendation!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was easy to find information when we arrived in Sydney. Macquarie University was very good at sending emails with information, introduction programs, and similar practical details. We did experience some minor issues when arranging our timetable, as we moved things around quite a bit to try to fit all our classes into one day per week. However, the university staff were very helpful at the IT desk, and we ended up with a good solution.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We signed up for Macquarie University’s introduction program during Orientation Week. We were shown around the campus and had various practical matters explained to us by older students. It was very helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was relatively easy to find accommodation. We initially had an arrangement with a man who owned a large house where many Danes often live, and we had received his contact details in advance through an acquaintance. However, once we arrived, we decided that we did not want to live there. We then used
flatmates.com
and found available rooms in a large shared house, which worked out quite easily. It also seems to be easier to find accommodation in July (Australian winter) compared to January (Australian summer).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is great to live close to a public transport hub. We lived in Bondi Junction, which made a lot of sense in terms of taking the train to the university while also being close to the beach and the ocean. In addition, it is important to be aware that many rents increase during the summer period, so you should keep in mind that the rent may change. Many houses in the Bondi area struggle with issues such as mould, rats outside, and similar problems. The housing standard is somewhat different from what you may be used to in Copenhagen, so this is something to be aware of.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Our house was quite worn down and not very clean. Our landlord did not do much to address the issues, which is why I would rate it 3 out of 5.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was quite easy to enrol in courses at Macquarie University. You can design your own timetable, which is really great. It is also possible to choose online courses, and all lectures are available online. However, it is important to be aware that many courses fill up quickly, so if you want flexibility in putting together a good timetable, you should secure a spot in your preferred class day and time as early as possible.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: After the University of Copenhagen had approved the courses, you applied to enrol in them at Macquarie University. Some courses required filling out a waiver request, where Macquarie needed to approve that you met the prerequisites for the course. After that, you could register for the course on a day and time of your choice, based on the options offered.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could contact Macquarie via their IT portal from home in Denmark. It was also possible to speak with the IT desk in person at Macquarie after arrival.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I enrolled in the courses I wanted (three mandatory courses and one elective). I had three classes back-to-back on Wednesdays and one online class on Tuesday evening. This worked really well and gave me a lot of free time outside of class.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to apply for a waiver at Macquarie as soon as the University of Copenhagen has approved your courses — this will give you the most options to choose from. If you wait to enrol in courses at Macquarie, you risk only having limited options, such as Tuesday evenings from 7–9 PM or Saturdays.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In general, I didn’t think the teaching was very good. This might be because I took courses at Macquarie Business School even though I study psychology, as the University of Copenhagen had approved Organizational and Work Psychology as a business course at Macquarie. As a result, it wasn’t exactly equivalent, since I was studying on a different campus in Australia.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took two first-year courses and two third-year courses at the BA level. The first-year courses were somewhat lower in level than in Denmark — most of the work focused on reflecting on your own role in the subject. The third-year courses were more comparable to those in Denmark.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In general, all the lectures were online (you could apparently also attend them in person, but I didn’t). The courses were very similar to a seminar at the University of Copenhagen, with a class of around 30 students where you discuss topics, give presentations, and work on projects together.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Indigenous people in Australia (elective course)
Introduction to Human Resource Management (mandatory course)
Managing Change in Organisations (mandatory course)
Social Research Methods (mandatory course) - This course has now been discontinued and was a replacement for Avanceret forskningsdesign og videnskabsteori (7,5 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Indigenous people in Australia! It was a really interesting and rewarding course. It provided a great historical understanding of living in Australia and the country’s history. It gave a deeper insight into many of the conflicts that exist in the country and offered some valuable reflections along the way. The lecturer was skilled and very engaged.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: We travelled a lot and that was expensive but very worth it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: We were four danish students who bought a car for 44.000 DKK. We sold it for 26.320 DKK. We lost more money than expected on this.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not attend any clubs or anything. But there is a lot of opportunities at Macquarie (we got the introduction in O-week).

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: So many different things. All kinds of athletic activities. Lots of social clubs and cultural as well.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I didn't attend any.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Visit the Pacific Islands and New Zealand.
I can recommend buying a car with friends. It gives opportunity for many weekend trips around NSW, camping trips etc. We loved it!
Tasmania was amazing!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Sydney is such a nice city. We lived in Bondi and you should be aware that there is an extremely strong body-conscious culture around Bondi. It might be triggering for some people, but you get used to it.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Run clubs!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There is not really a night life in Sydney. It is definitely a morning city. Everyone is up and working out at 5 am. And all clubs close around midnight or 1 AM.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The morning culture was amazing, I loved it. The aussie's are so nice people, and I loved how open and social the culture is. I loved the small talk everywhere you go. The culture around the coast line is amazing with beaches and surfing vibes.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Live closer to the beach and not on campus around Macquarie. You will spend most time around inner Sydney/eastern suburbs. 
2. Try to collect the classes on one or two day and give yourself as much time as possible to enjoy Sydney
3. If you have an elective course, do the Indigenous people in Australia. It was so rewarding.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living so close with my friends, being each other’s primary people on the other side of the world, caring so much for one another, and making sure we were all doing well — it felt very much like a family with friends. I learned a lot from moving far away from home, but the best part was that it happened with good friends.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I felt that the culture in Sydney could sometimes feel unpredictable. Everyone is very self-aware and focused on their own personal growth. It was difficult to deal with the fact that you couldn’t always rely on other people. It’s not very Danish.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
